teile.einleitung: A physical map shows the surface of the Earth with mountains, valleys, rivers and seas. With colours it shows how high the land is or how deep the water is. In contrast, a political map shows countries and borders.
wichtigste: A physical map uses colours to show how high the land is.
Green stands for low, flat land, yellow for land of medium height.
Brown shows high mountains: the darker, the higher.
White stands for glaciers and ice in high mountains.
Dark blue shows deep sea, light blue shallow water.
A political map, by contrast, shows countries and borders.
The Swiss national map shows mountains with shading.

abschnitte.text: The **physical map** shows what the Earth’s surface looks like: where mountains, valleys, plains, rivers and seas lie. With **colours** it shows the height of the land. A **political map**, by contrast, shows countries and borders. There, neighbouring countries have different colours so that they are easy to tell apart. Many atlases contain both kinds of map.

The colours follow a fixed series. **Green** shows low areas, usually plains and valleys. Above that comes **yellow** for land of medium height. **Brown** stands for high mountains: the higher the land, the darker the brown. That is why the Alps are drawn in brown. At the very top, **white** stands for snow, **glaciers** and ice. What each colour means exactly is explained in the map’s **key**.

Water also has different shades. **Light blue** shows shallow water, for example close to the coast. **Dark blue** shows deep water, for example in the middle of the oceans. Greenland usually appears **white** on physical maps, because most of it is covered by thick ice. So is Antarctica.

The **national map of Switzerland** is published by the Federal Office of Topography, **swisstopo**. Its mountains look almost real because they are **shaded**. The map behaves as if light were coming from the top left. As a result, slopes look light on one side and dark on the other, and the terrain looks three-dimensional. **Forests** are coloured green on the national map.

gewusst: A green area on a physical map does not necessarily mean that a lot grows there. A low-lying desert can also be drawn in green.
The shading on Swiss national maps is known around the world for its beauty and accuracy.

teile.einleitung: The Philippines is an island state in South-East Asia in the western Pacific. It is made up of more than 7,000 islands and has a long history as a Spanish and later American colony. The country is known for its nature, but also for frequent typhoons.
wichtigste: The Philippines is made up of more than 7,000 islands.
The capital is Manila on the island of Luzon.
Luzon is the largest island, Mindanao the second largest.
The name comes from the Spanish King Philip II.
In 1898 the Philippines passed from Spain to the USA, and in 1946 they became independent.
The great majority of people are Roman Catholic.
Every year several typhoons sweep across the country.

abschnitte.text: The Philippines is made up of **more than 7,000 islands**. Many of them are small and uninhabited. The largest and most populous island is **Luzon** in the north. The capital **Manila**, a very densely populated city, lies there. The second largest island is **Mindanao** in the south. In 2020 more than 100 million people lived in the Philippines.

In 1521 the navigator **Ferdinand Magellan** reached the islands. Later they were named after **Philip II**, who became King of Spain. Spain ruled the Philippines for more than 300 years. After the **Spanish-American War** of 1898 they became a colony of the **USA**. Only in 1946 did the Philippines become an **independent** state.

Many different languages are spoken in the Philippines. The national languages are **Filipino** and **English**. Because of the long Spanish colonial period, the great majority of the population is **Roman Catholic**. The Philippines is the largest Catholic country in Asia. In the south, especially on Mindanao, many Muslims also live.

In the Philippines live many animals that are found nowhere else. The **Philippine tarsier** is only as big as a hand but has huge eyes. On the island of **Bohol** stand more than 1,000 round hills, the **Chocolate Hills**. In the dry season their grass turns brown, and then they look like chocolate. The country lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire and therefore also has volcanoes.

A typical means of transport is the **jeepney**. These brightly painted shared taxis were originally built from old military jeeps. A great danger for the country is **typhoons**. A typhoon is a powerful tropical storm over the Pacific. Every year several typhoons sweep across the Philippines and bring storms and heavy rain.

gewusst: Ferdinand Magellan died in the Philippines in 1521, on the small island of Mactan. His fleet sailed on without him and was the first to sail around the world.
The Philippine tarsier can turn its head very far, almost like an owl.

teile.einleitung: Petra is an ancient city in the south of Jordan whose houses, tombs and temples were carved straight into the rock walls. The Nabataeans built it more than 2,000 years ago. Today Petra is one of the most famous sights in the world.
wichtigste: Petra is a city carved into the rock in Jordan.
The sandstone glows red and pink, which is why Petra is also called the rose-red city.
Most people enter Petra through a narrow gorge, the Siq.
The most famous building is the Treasury with its magnificent façade.
The Nabataeans grew rich through trade in frankincense and spices.
In AD 106 the area became part of the Roman Empire.
Petra has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.

abschnitte.text: Petra lies in a valley between mountains of **sandstone**. The inhabitants did not build their houses and tombs up from stones, but cut them straight into the rock walls. The stone glows in red, pink and orange, especially beautifully at sunset. That is why Petra is also called the **rose-red city**. The name Petra comes from Greek and means “rock”.

Petra was founded by the **Nabataeans**, an Arab people. Their city lay on important trade routes. Through Petra passed **caravans** of camels bringing frankincense from southern Arabia and spices to the Mediterranean. The Nabataeans charged customs duties and grew rich as a result. In AD 106 the Emperor **Trajan** made their kingdom the Roman province of Arabia.

The way into the city leads through the **Siq**, a narrow gorge with high rock walls. At its end the **Treasury** suddenly appears, a façade with columns about 2,000 years old, carved into the rock. High above the city lies the **Monastery**, in Arabic ad-Deir. About 800 steps lead up to it. It is one of the largest rock-cut buildings in Petra.

In the area around Petra it rarely rains. Even so, many people lived here. The Nabataeans were masters at handling water. They collected rainwater in **channels** and **conduits** and led it into large **cisterns**, which are underground water stores. This meant they had enough to drink even in the dry season.

After the Middle Ages Petra was forgotten in Europe. In 1812 **Johann Ludwig Burckhardt** came there, a traveller from a Basel family. He travelled through the Middle East in Arab clothing and was the first European of his time to report on the rock city. Since 1985 Petra has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and is visited by very many people every year.

gewusst: The Treasury of Petra can be seen in the 1989 film “Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade”.
In 2007 Petra was chosen in a worldwide vote as one of the “New Seven Wonders of the World”.

teile.einleitung: A mushroom rock is a rock with a broad head and a narrow base that looks like a mushroom. Shapes like this form mainly in deserts, where the wind hurls grains of sand against the foot of the rock. Similar-looking shapes also exist in Switzerland, but they came about in a different way.
wichtigste: Mushroom rocks have a broad cap and a narrow stem.
The wind wears away mainly the foot of the rock with sand.
Most sand grains bounce close to the ground.
A hard cap layer above softer rock favours the mushroom shape.
Salt weathering can weaken the damp foot even more.
The White Desert in Egypt is known for its mushroom rocks.
The earth pyramids of Euseigne in the Valais were formed by rain.

abschnitte.titel: Like a mushroom made of stone
abschnitte.text: A **mushroom rock** has a broad **cap** at the top and a narrow **stem** below. Often there is a hard, resistant layer of rock on top. Underneath, the rock is softer. The soft layer is worn away faster than the hard one. Over time this produces the typical mushroom shape. Mushroom rocks are one of the forms of **wind erosion**, that is, wearing away by wind.

In deserts the wind carries **grains of sand** with it. Because they are heavy, it lifts them only a little way. Most grains bounce **close to the ground**. There they act like a sandblaster and wear away the foot of the rock more than the upper part. This is called **sand abrasion** or **corrasion**. Close to the ground the rock is also often damper and richer in salt. **Salt weathering** loosens it, and the wind carries it away more easily.

Famous mushroom rocks stand in the **White Desert** in Egypt, near the oasis of Farafra. There the wind has ground white **chalk and limestone rocks** into astonishing shapes. Many look like mushrooms, others remind you of animals. Other forms of wind erosion are **yardangs**, long streamlined rock ridges, and **ventifacts**, stones with sharp edges and smooth faces, for example three-edged stones (dreikanters).

In the Valais stand the **earth pyramids of Euseigne** in the Val d’Hérens. They look similar to mushroom rocks: tall pillars with a large stone as a cap. But they were not formed by wind. **Rain** has worn away soft **moraine material** that a glacier left behind. Pillars remained standing only where large capstones protected the material.

gewusst: The road into the Val d’Hérens passes through a short tunnel right through the earth pyramids at Euseigne.
If the capstone of an earth pyramid falls off, the pillar is quickly worn away by the rain.

teile.einleitung: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen all the time. It is found in the polar regions and in high mountains, including the Swiss Alps. Because the Earth is warming, it is thawing in many places, with consequences for the landscape, the climate and safety.
wichtigste: About a quarter of the land area of the Northern Hemisphere lies above permafrost.
In Switzerland around 5 per cent of the country’s area is affected.
Permafrost soils store about twice as much carbon as the atmosphere.
When ice-rich ground thaws, it sinks and thermokarst forms.
Rock glaciers are a visible sign of permafrost.
The PERMOS network monitors permafrost in the Swiss Alps.

abschnitte.text: About **24 per cent** of the land area of the Northern Hemisphere lies above permafrost, so roughly a quarter. There are large areas in **Siberia**, Canada, Alaska and on the **Tibetan Plateau**. In high mountains too, the ground is often permanently frozen. In **Switzerland**, according to model calculations by the Federal Office for the Environment, this affects about **5 per cent** of the country’s area. That is more than the area of all Swiss glaciers put together.

In the Alps, permafrost is found mainly in rock faces and scree slopes at high altitude. A visible sign is **rock glaciers**: tongue-shaped masses of rock debris with ice inside, which creep slowly down the valley. Many of them now move much faster than they used to. The Swiss monitoring network **PERMOS** (Permafrost Monitoring Switzerland) measures, among other things, temperatures in boreholes. Above **Pontresina** in the Engadine, large protective dams against debris flows and avalanches were built on the Schafberg in 2003.

If frozen ground contains a lot of ice, it loses its support as it thaws. The surface sags unevenly. Hollows, pools and lakes form. This kind of landscape is called **thermokarst**. The water in the hollows stores heat and speeds up the thawing even more. A well-known example is the **Batagaika crater** in Yakutia in north-eastern Siberia. It is more than a kilometre long and has been growing for decades, because its edges thaw and break off.

In the northern permafrost soils an estimated **1,400 to 1,600 gigatonnes of carbon** are stored. That is about twice as much as in today’s atmosphere. The carbon is held in old, frozen plant remains. When the ground thaws, **microbes** can turn it into **CO2 and methane**. These gases strengthen the warming, which in turn makes more permafrost thaw.

Disease-causing germs can also survive for a long time in frozen ground. In 2016 **anthrax** broke out on the **Yamal** Peninsula in Siberia. During a heatwave, an infected, frozen reindeer carcass had thawed. The spores had survived in the ground and caused an outbreak among reindeer and people.

gewusst: There is more permafrost area in Switzerland than there is glacier area in the whole country.
In Siberia only the top layer of soil thaws in summer, and below it the ground stays frozen all year round.

teile.einleitung: The Peters projection is a way of showing the round Earth on a flat world map. It shows all countries at their correct size in relation to one another. In return, the shapes of the countries look badly distorted.
wichtigste: The Peters projection is equal-area.
Regions of the same size appear the same size on it.
In return, the shapes of the countries are badly distorted.
James Gall had already described the same projection in 1855.
That is why it is often called the Gall-Peters projection.
Arno Peters made it known from 1973.

abschnitte.titel: The problem of every world map
abschnitte.text: The Earth is a sphere. If you want to put it on a flat sheet, you have to distort it. The method for doing this is called a **map projection**. No map can show areas, shapes and angles correctly all at once. The widely used **Mercator map** is **conformal** (it keeps angles true) and is handy for sailing. But it greatly enlarges regions near the poles. On it Greenland looks almost as big as Africa, although Africa is about fourteen times bigger.

abschnitte.titel: True to area instead of true to shape
abschnitte.text: The Peters projection is an **equal-area cylindrical projection**. Regions of the same size also appear the same size on it. In return, the **shapes** are badly distorted. Countries near the equator, such as those in Africa, look stretched out lengthways. Regions near the poles look squashed flat.

The German **Arno Peters** presented the map from 1973. He argued that the Mercator map enlarges Europe and North America and makes the countries of the **global South** look too small. His map was therefore spread by **development organisations** and churches. But the same projection had already been described in 1855 by the Scottish clergyman **James Gall**. Peters did not mention him. That is why people often speak of the **Gall-Peters projection**.

Many **cartographers** criticise the Peters projection because of the strong distortion of shapes. They also point out that other equal-area maps existed before it. For world maps many prefer **compromise projections**, which show neither areas nor shapes quite exactly, but show both reasonably well. One example is the **Winkel tripel projection**, which many atlases also use.

gewusst: On the Mercator map Greenland looks about as big as Africa, but in reality Africa is about fourteen times bigger.
Only a globe shows areas, shapes and angles all correctly at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Physical weathering, also called mechanical weathering, breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemical make-up. The causes are mainly changes in temperature, frost, salts, release of pressure and plant roots. It prepares the ground for chemical weathering.
wichtigste: In physical weathering rock breaks up, but the minerals stay the same.
Insolation weathering is caused by strong temperature swings between day and night.
It is especially effective in deserts.
Exfoliation is the flaking off of rock in curved layers after pressure is released.
Root wedging is caused by roots growing in cracks.
Broken-up rock gives chemical weathering more surface to attack.
Granite often crumbles into grus or into rounded woolsack blocks.

abschnitte.text: In **physical weathering** rock is only broken into smaller pieces. Its **minerals** stay unchanged. In **chemical weathering**, by contrast, the minerals are changed or dissolved by water and dissolved substances. The two processes often work together. Physical weathering increases the **surface** of the rock, so that chemical weathering can attack in more places.

In **deserts** the surface of the rock heats up strongly by day and cools down at night, because there are no clouds or plants. The repeated expansion and shrinking creates stresses. This **insolation weathering** makes the rock crumbly. In the Alps **frost wedging** is especially important: water seeps into cracks, freezes and expands by about nine per cent as it does so. The large **scree slopes** beneath Swiss rock faces are formed mainly in this way.

In **salt weathering**, salt crystals grow in pores and cracks and push the rock apart. A related form is **hydration weathering**. In it, certain minerals, such as some salts, build water molecules into their **crystal lattice** and expand. The pressure loosens the rock. It must be clearly distinguished from **hydrolysis**, a kind of chemical weathering.

Deep underground, rock is under great pressure. When the rock above it is worn away, the rock expands. As it does so, layers come away parallel to the surface, rather like an onion. This is called **exfoliation**. Granite also often weathers along its joints. The edges are attacked most strongly, and rounded blocks form, which are called **woolsacks**.

Plants can also break up rock. Roots grow into joints and press on the rock as they get thicker. This **root wedging** counts as physical-biological weathering. When **granite** breaks up into its separate grains of quartz, feldspar and mica, a coarse, loose debris forms. This material is called **grus**.

gewusst: The force of freezing water in a closed crack is so great that it can split even hard granite.
Well-known woolsack blocks of granite can be found, for example, in the Fichtelgebirge and the Harz in Germany.

teile.einleitung: The Persian Gulf is a marginal sea of the Indian Ocean between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula. On its coasts lie some of the largest oil deposits in the world. That is why it is very important for the world economy.
wichtigste: As a marginal sea, the Persian Gulf belongs to the Indian Ocean.
The Strait of Hormuz connects it with the Gulf of Oman.
Iran lies along the whole northern shore, Arab states along the southern shore.
Bahrain is an island state in the Gulf, Qatar a peninsula.
Before oil, many people lived from pearl fishing.
Ghawar in Saudi Arabia is the largest conventional oil field in the world.

abschnitte.text: The Persian Gulf is linked to the **Indian Ocean** by the **Gulf of Oman** and the Arabian Sea. **Iran** owns the whole of the northern coast. On the southern shore lie Arab states such as Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. **Bahrain** is an island state off the coast of Saudi Arabia with the capital Manama. **Qatar** juts into the Gulf as a small peninsula, and its capital is Doha.

The Gulf is connected to the open sea only by a narrow channel: the **Strait of Hormuz**. At its narrowest point it is only about 40 kilometres wide. Many **oil tankers** pass through here, which is why it is one of the most important shipping routes in the world. Saudi Arabia has built an **east-west pipeline** to the port of **Yanbu** on the Red Sea. This means part of the oil can still be exported even if the sea route through the Gulf is blocked.

Before oil was found, many people on the Gulf lived from **pearl fishing**. Divers brought up oysters with pearls from the sea bed. Cultured pearls and oil later replaced this trade. In 1908, at **Masjed Soleyman** in Persia, today’s Iran, the first commercially important oil in the Middle East was found. From this grew the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, the forerunner of **BP**.

On the Gulf lie some of the largest oil deposits on Earth. The **Ghawar field** in eastern Saudi Arabia is the largest conventional oil field in the world and about 280 kilometres long. In the **United Arab Emirates**, about 95 per cent of the oil reserves lie in the emirate of **Abu Dhabi**. **Dubai** produced comparatively little oil and turned early to trade, tourism and finance.

The name “Persian Gulf” comes from Persia, the old name of Iran. In Arab countries the name **“Arabian Gulf”** is often used. There has long been a dispute between the neighbouring countries over the correct name. In English “Persian Gulf” is the usual name.

gewusst: The Persian Gulf is quite shallow, less than 50 metres deep in many places.
The water in the Gulf is especially salty, because a lot of water evaporates in the heat.

teile.einleitung: The rock city of Petra lies in the south of Jordan, in a valley near the town of Wadi Musa. It has a long and exciting history: from the Nabataeans through a severe earthquake to the Bedouins, who were still living in its caves only a few decades ago.
wichtigste: At the entrance to Petra lies the town of Wadi Musa, which means “Valley of Moses”.
The Siq is a narrow rock gorge more than a kilometre long.
In AD 363 an earthquake badly damaged many buildings.
Johann Ludwig Burckhardt travelled to Petra disguised as Sheikh Ibrahim.
The Arabic script developed from the script of the Nabataeans.
Until the 1980s Bedouins lived in the caves of Petra.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who visits Petra usually stays the night in the town of **Wadi Musa**. The name means “Valley of Moses”. From there you walk through the **Siq**. This gorge is more than a kilometre long and in some places only a few metres wide. The rock walls tower high into the sky on the left and right. At the end the view opens up onto the famous Treasury.

The **Nabataeans** developed Petra into their capital. They had their own **script**, which is found on inscriptions all over the area. Over time the letters changed more and more. The **Arabic script**, which very many people in the world use today, eventually developed from the Nabataean script.

In AD 363 a strong **earthquake** shook the region. Many free-standing buildings and water pipes were destroyed. After that Petra lost more and more importance, also because the trade routes had shifted. The façades cut into the rock survived the quake much better than the houses built of masonry.

In Europe, people long knew hardly anything about Petra. **Johann Ludwig Burckhardt**, a traveller from a Basel family, learned Arabic and passed himself off as a Muslim scholar, **Sheikh Ibrahim**. This way he was able to reach Petra unrecognised in 1812. His reports made the rock city known in Europe.

For a long time a **Bedouin tribe** lived in the old rock caves of Petra. Bedouins are people who traditionally travel through the desert with their animals. When Petra became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985, the families moved to a new village nearby. Many of them now work in tourism, for example with donkeys, camels or sales stalls.

gewusst: At the top of the Treasury façade stands a stone urn. Bedouins thought it held gold and shot at it. You can still see the bullet holes today, but the urn is made of solid stone.
In Arabic the Treasury is called al-Khazneh. But no treasure was ever found there.

teile.einleitung: A permafrost soil is ground that stays frozen for a long time. It is found in cold regions such as Siberia, Canada and the high mountains. When it thaws, it becomes soft and unstable.
wichtigste: Permafrost stays below 0 °C without a break for at least two years.
The top layer thaws in summer and is called the active layer.
Permafrost lies beneath about a quarter of the land area of the Northern Hemisphere.
In Switzerland it occurs on about 5 per cent of the country’s area.
When it thaws in the Alps, rockfalls and rockslides increase.
When it thaws, greenhouse gases such as methane are released.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **permafrost** when ground or rock stays colder than 0 °C **for at least two years** without a break. The word is made up of “permanent”, meaning lasting, and “frost”. Above the frozen ground lies the **active layer**. It thaws every summer and freezes again in winter. It is often only a few decimetres to a few metres thick.

Permafrost lies beneath about a quarter of the land area of the Northern Hemisphere. It is most widespread in **Siberia**, Alaska, Canada and on the Tibetan Plateau. In eastern Siberia the ground is frozen in some places to a depth of about **1,500 metres**. Some of this frost dates from the **Ice Ages**. In Switzerland permafrost occurs on about 5 per cent of the country’s area, mainly in scree slopes and rock faces above about 2,500 metres.

Frozen water in cracks in the rock acts like **cement** and holds the stone together. When it gets warmer and the ice thaws, the rock loses this hold. Then **rockfalls** and **rockslides** increase, and debris can slip away. That is why experts in Switzerland keep a close watch on endangered mountain slopes. Mountain railways and huts built on permafrost also have to be well secured.

In **Siberia** many houses stand on **stilts**. A heated house built directly on the ground would thaw the permafrost beneath it. The ground would turn soft, and the house could sink or crack. This way cold air can flow underneath the house. Roads and pipelines are also hard to build in such areas.

Huge amounts of **dead plant remains** are frozen in permafrost. When they thaw, **microorganisms** break them down. This produces **carbon dioxide** and **methane**. These greenhouse gases strengthen the warming of the Earth. Experts speak of a feedback loop: warmth makes permafrost thaw, and the thawing brings even more warmth.

gewusst: In Siberia, well-preserved mammoths from the Ice Age have been found in the permafrost.
Permafrost can even lie beneath the sea floor of the Arctic.

teile.einleitung: A pile dwelling is a house that stands on piles so that its floor is higher than the ground or the water. In Switzerland, people were building villages like this on lake shores more than 6,000 years ago. Pile dwellings also exist today in many parts of the world.
wichtigste: A pile dwelling is a house on wooden piles.
Piles protect the house from floods and damp.
In Switzerland the old pile-dwelling villages lay on lake shores and in bogs.
The first pile-dwelling villages appeared in the Neolithic period.
Under water and mud, wood and tools were preserved.
Since 2011 the pile dwellings around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Venice, too, stands on many wooden piles.

abschnitte.text: To build a pile dwelling, long **piles** are driven into the ground. The house stands on top of them. This puts the floor of the house higher than its surroundings. If the water rises in a **flood**, the house stays dry. The old piles were made of **wood**, and the houses were made of wood, clay and reeds.

As early as the **Neolithic period**, more than 6,000 years ago, people in Switzerland built villages on the shores of lakes and in bogs. They were already **farmers**: they grew grain and kept animals. Many remains were found, for example, on **Lake Zurich**, **Lake Biel** and Lake Neuchâtel. In the later Bronze Age, too, people lived in villages like this.

Why do we know so much about these villages? The remains lay for a long time **under water and mud**. There is no air there, so wood, seeds, cloth and tools rotted only very slowly. That is why archaeologists still find piles, clay pots and even leftover food today. From the wood of the piles it is often possible to read off exactly which year a tree was felled.

In 2011 the **prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps** were added to the **UNESCO World Heritage** list. Prehistoric means: from the time before there were written records. The sites lie in six countries. Many of them, about half, are in Switzerland. Most cannot be seen from outside, because they lie under water or in the ground.

People still build on piles today. In the **tropics** many houses stand on **stilts**, because it often rains and the ground is wet. This keeps the house dry and makes it harder for animals to get in. The Italian city of **Venice** was built in a lagoon. Its houses stand on a very large number of wooden piles that are driven deep into the ground.

gewusst: In the winter of 1853/54 Lake Zurich had dropped especially low. At Meilen old piles came to light, and in Switzerland a great enthusiasm for the pile-dwellers began.
Wood that lies in water without air can last for thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: Pinatubo is a volcano on the island of Luzon in the Philippines. In June 1991 it erupted after about 500 years of rest. It was one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the 20th century, and it even cooled the climate of the whole Earth for a short time.
wichtigste: Pinatubo lies in the west of Luzon, about 90 km north-west of Manila.
Before 1991 it had rested for about 500 years.
The main eruption was on 15 June 1991, and the ash column rose about 35 km high.
The eruption reached 6 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index.
At the same time Typhoon Yunya passed over the area.
Afterwards the Earth’s temperature fell temporarily by about 0.5 degrees.
Timely evacuations saved thousands of lives.

abschnitte.text: **Pinatubo** lies in the west of the island of **Luzon**, about 90 km north-west of the capital Manila. Its last major eruption was about **500 years** earlier. The mountain was thickly forested, and many people hardly knew it was a volcano. In spring 1991 the ground began to shake, and steam and gases rose from the mountain.

After weeks of growing activity, the main eruption came on **15 June 1991**. The **eruption column** of ash and gas rose about 35 km high. The volcano threw out about 10 km³ of material and reached **VEI 6** on the **Volcanic Explosivity Index**. This scale measures how violent an eruption is. On the same day **Typhoon Yunya** passed over the area. Its rain soaked the ash and made it very heavy, so that many roofs collapsed.

Philippine and American experts watched the volcano closely. They analysed **earthquakes** and **gas measurements** and gave an early warning. **Tens of thousands** of people were brought to safety before the main eruption. The nearby **Clark Air Base**, a large base of the US Air Force, was also evacuated. Because of the heavy damage, the USA gave it up afterwards. The forecast is regarded as a great success for **volcanology**.

The volcano blew about 15 to 20 million tonnes of **sulphur dioxide** up into the **stratosphere**, a high layer of the atmosphere. From this, tiny floating particles formed, the **sulphate aerosols**. They spread around the Earth and reflected part of the sunlight back into space. In 1992 and 1993 it was about **0.5 degrees** cooler worldwide.

During the eruption the summit collapsed, and a **caldera** formed, a large basin about 2.5 km wide. The mountain became clearly lower as a result. Monsoon rains gradually filled the caldera with water. This created **Lake Pinatubo**, which today is also visited by tourists. For years after the eruption, rain washed ash down into the valley as mudflows called **lahars**.

gewusst: After the eruption of Pinatubo, strikingly coloured sunsets were also seen in Europe, because the fine particles high in the air scattered the light.
Pinatubo lost several hundred metres of height in the eruption.

teile.einleitung: Pikes Peak is a well-known mountain in the US state of Colorado. It belongs to the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains and towers above the city of Colorado Springs. It is famous for a song, a cog railway and a car race.
wichtigste: Pikes Peak lies in Colorado in the USA.
It is about 4,300 metres high and belongs to the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains.
It is named after the explorer Zebulon Pike.
Katharine Lee Bates wrote the poem “America the Beautiful” there in 1893.
A road and a cog railway lead to the summit.

abschnitte.text: **Pikes Peak** is about **4,300 metres** high, so only slightly lower than the highest peaks of the Swiss Alps. It belongs to the **Front Range**, the easternmost chain of the **Rocky Mountains**. Because it rises on its own above the flat prairie, it can be seen from far away. At the foot of the mountain lies the city of **Colorado Springs**.

The mountain is named after **Zebulon Pike**. This American officer explored the area in 1806. He did not reach the summit itself at that time. Later, during the Colorado gold rush, the mountain became a well-known landmark for settlers.

In 1893 the teacher and poet **Katharine Lee Bates** climbed Pikes Peak. The wide view over the land delighted her so much that she wrote the poem **“America the Beautiful”**. Later it was set to music. Today it is one of the best-known **patriotic songs** in the USA.

A **cog railway** leads to the summit, one of the highest in the world. Its railcars were built in **Switzerland**. There is also a road all the way to the top. Since 1916 the **Pikes Peak International Hill Climb** has been held on it, a famous mountain race for cars and motorcycles.

gewusst: At the summit of Pikes Peak the air is so thin that some visitors get a headache.
After the Indianapolis 500, the Pikes Peak hill climb is one of the oldest motor races in the USA.

teile.einleitung: Beijing, called Peking in German, is the capital of the People’s Republic of China and one of the largest cities in the world. The city is known for its old imperial palaces, temples and modern buildings.
wichtigste: Beijing is the capital of the People’s Republic of China.
“Beijing” means “northern capital”.
The Chinese emperors used to live in the Forbidden City.
The Summer Olympic Games took place in Beijing in 2008.
Beijing was the first city to host both the Summer and the Winter Games.
Also well known are the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace and the hutongs.

abschnitte.text: Beijing lies in the north of China. The Chinese name **Beijing** is made up of “bei”, meaning **north**, and “jing”, meaning **capital**. For many centuries Chinese emperors ruled from here. Today Beijing is the seat of the government of the **People’s Republic of China** and an important centre of culture and science.

In the centre lies the **Forbidden City**, a huge old **imperial palace**. The emperors once lived there with their court. Ordinary people were not allowed in, hence the name. Today it is a museum. In the north-west of the city lies the **Summer Palace** with Kunming Lake, hills and pavilions. The emperors spent the hot months there. It is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

At the **Temple of Heaven** the emperors prayed for a good **harvest**. The round hall with the blue roof is a landmark of the city. In the old town there are narrow, traditional alleys with courtyard houses. They are called **hutongs**. Many were pulled down, and some are now protected as part of the city’s history.

In 2008 the **Summer Olympic Games** took place in Beijing. The opening ceremony began on 8.8.2008, because eight is seen as a lucky number in China. The **National Stadium** was built for the Games. Because of its interwoven steel beams it is called the **“Bird’s Nest”**. In 2022 Beijing also hosted the Winter Games. This made it the first city in the world to have held both kinds of Olympic Games.

A famous dish is named after the city: **Peking duck**. The duck is roasted so that the skin becomes especially crisp. It is eaten cut into pieces with thin **pancakes**, cucumber, spring onions and a sweet sauce.

gewusst: Not far from Beijing runs the Great Wall of China, which you can visit from the city on a day trip.
The Forbidden City is one of the largest palace complexes in the world.

teile.einleitung: A pipeline is a long pipe through which crude oil, natural gas, water or other substances flow over long distances. Pipelines connect production sites with ports, refineries and cities. An important gas pipeline also runs through Switzerland.
wichtigste: A pipeline is a long pipe for oil, gas or other substances.
The Druzhba pipeline brings Russian crude oil to central Europe; Druzhba means friendship.
The Trans-Alaska Pipeline runs about 1,300 km to the port of Valdez.
The Transitgas pipeline crosses Switzerland from Wallbach to the Gries Pass.
In September 2022 explosions damaged the Nord Stream pipelines in the Baltic Sea.
A pig is used to clean and inspect pipelines.

abschnitte.text: A **pipeline** is made up of many steel pipes welded together. Pumps or compressors push crude oil or natural gas through the line. Pipelines often lie underground, on supports above the ground or on the sea bed. They can be thousands of kilometres long. For large amounts over land this is usually cheaper than transport by lorry or train.

The **Transitgas pipeline** begins at **Wallbach** on the High Rhine in the canton of Aargau. It crosses the Alps partly in tunnels and is connected to the Italian network near the **Gries Pass**. In the past the gas flowed only from northern Europe to Italy. Since the **reverse-flow conversion**, completed in 2017, it can also flow from south to north. This increases security of supply.

The **Druzhba pipeline** was built in the 1960s, and its name is Russian for “friendship”. It supplied the Eastern Bloc states of the time with crude oil. The **Trans-Alaska Pipeline** runs about 1,300 km from the oil fields at Prudhoe Bay to the ice-free port of **Valdez**. Since 2019 the **“Power of Siberia”** pipeline has brought gas from eastern Siberia to **China**, and since 2020 the **Trans Adriatic Pipeline** has delivered gas from **Azerbaijan** to Italy.

Pipelines make countries dependent on one another: the supplying country on the buyer and the other way round. That is why they are often a topic in **politics**. In **September 2022** underwater explosions damaged three of the four strings of the **Nord Stream 1 and 2** pipelines in the Baltic Sea. Large amounts of gas escaped. New pipelines such as the TAP are meant to help reduce dependence on single suppliers.

To keep a pipeline safe, it has to be cleaned and inspected. For this a **pig** is sent through the line. This is a device that fits exactly into the pipe and is pushed forward by the oil or gas. Simple pigs push deposits out. **Smart pigs** measure the wall thickness on the way and find damage before a leak occurs.

gewusst: The Trans-Alaska Pipeline stands on supports in many places, so that the warm oil does not thaw the frozen ground.
In German the device is called a “Molch”, which means a newt: it slips through the pipe like one.

teile.einleitung: Peru is a country in the west of South America on the Pacific Ocean. It was once the centre of the Inca Empire. The country has deserts on the coast, high mountains in the Andes and rainforest in the east.
wichtigste: The capital of Peru is Lima, the largest city in the country.
Cusco used to be the capital of the Incas.
Quechua is an official language alongside Spanish.
The currency is called the sol.
The flag is red, white, red.
The famous Nazca Lines lie in the desert.

abschnitte.text: Peru has three very different landscapes. On the **coast** it is dry and there are deserts. The capital **Lima**, the largest city in the country, is also there. In the middle the high **Andes** run through the country. In the east the **Amazon rainforest** begins. Lake Titicaca on the border with Bolivia also belongs partly to Peru.

**Cusco** used to be the capital of the Inca Empire. The city lies high in the mountains at about 3,400 metres. Many walls from the Inca period still stand there today. Not far away lies the famous ruined city of **Machu Picchu**. The old Andean language **Quechua** has been spoken for centuries and is today an **official language** alongside Spanish. Millions of people still speak it.

In the desert in the south of Peru there are huge pictures in the ground: the **Nazca Lines**. They are more than 1,500 years old. They are best seen from the air. They show, for example, a monkey, a **hummingbird** and a spider. Why the people made them is still not fully understood.

The flag of Peru has three vertical stripes: **red, white, red**. Red and white are also the colours of the Swiss flag. In Peru people pay with the **sol**. In Spanish the word means “sun”. The sun was very important to the Incas, who worshipped the sun god Inti.

A famous dish is **ceviche**. For it, raw fish is marinated in **lime juice**. The juice firms up the fish, rather as cooking does. Many kinds of **potato** also come from Peru. People in the Andes had been growing them for a long time before the potato came to Europe and to Switzerland.

gewusst: In Peru there are thousands of different kinds of potato.
The Nazca Lines are so big that you cannot make out some of the figures from the ground at all.

teile.einleitung: The Peruvian anchovy is a small shoaling fish from the Pacific off Peru and Chile. It is caught in huge quantities, mainly for fishmeal and fish oil. It is also called anchoveta.
wichtigste: The Peruvian anchovy lives off the coasts of Peru and Chile.
It is also called anchoveta.
The cold Humboldt Current brings many nutrients and therefore plenty of food.
It is mainly processed into fishmeal and fish oil.
During the climate phenomenon El Niño, stocks often fall sharply.

abschnitte.titel: A small fish in huge shoals
abschnitte.text: The Peruvian anchovy is a slim, silvery fish and usually grows to barely 20 centimetres. It lives in large **shoals** near the surface of the water. Off the coast of Peru flows the cold **Humboldt Current**. It brings nutrient-rich water up from the depths. In it grows a lot of **plankton**, the food of the anchovies. This is how huge shoals come about.

abschnitte.titel: One of the biggest fisheries in the world
abschnitte.text: Hardly any other kind of fish is caught in such large amounts. Only a small part is eaten. Most of it is processed into **fishmeal** and **fish oil**. From these people make, for example, feed for farmed fish, pigs and chickens. Seabirds such as pelicans and cormorants also eat the anchovies. Their droppings, **guano**, used to be mined as a valuable fertiliser.

During **El Niño** the water off Peru becomes warmer, and fewer nutrients rise to the surface. Then the anchovies find less food, and stocks fall sharply. In the early 1970s the catch collapsed dramatically after overfishing and an El Niño. Since then Peru has set **catch limits** to protect the stocks.

gewusst: In some years more Peruvian anchovy was caught than any other kind of fish in the world.
Part of the fish feed used in fish farms around the world comes from these small fish from Peru.

teile.einleitung: Poison dart frogs are small, brightly coloured frogs from the rainforests of Central and South America. Their skin contains poison, and their colours warn enemies of it. Some species are among the most poisonous animals in the world.
wichtigste: Poison dart frogs live in the rainforests of Central and South America.
Most are only about 1.5 to 5 centimetres long.
Their poison is in the skin.
The bright colours warn enemies.
The poison comes from their food, for example from ants and mites.
In zoos they become harmless because they are given other food.
The golden poison frog is among the most poisonous animals in the world.

abschnitte.text: Most poison dart frogs are only **1.5 to 5 centimetres** long, and many are shorter than a thumb. They glow in yellow, red, blue, green or orange, often with black spots. These bright colours are called **warning colours**. They tell enemies: Watch out, I am poisonous! That is why many animals leave them alone. Unlike many frogs, they are often out and about during the day.

Poison dart frogs live in the damp **rainforests** of Central and South America, most species in **South America**. They stay on the forest floor, among leaves and on plants. There they eat tiny animals such as **ants**, mites and small beetles. The damp, warm air is important for their delicate skin.

The **poison** is in the frogs’ **skin**. Anyone who eats or licks them can become ill. The surprising thing is that the frogs do not make the poison entirely themselves. They take in certain substances with their food, above all from ants and mites, and make their poison from them. In a **zoo** they are given other food and so usually become **harmless**.

Indigenous peoples in South America rubbed the poison of some species onto their **hunting darts**. This let them bring down animals. That is where the name poison dart frog comes from. Especially dangerous is the **golden poison frog** from **Colombia**. It is often bright yellow, and even a very small amount of its poison is dangerous.

Many poison dart frogs lay their eggs on land, for example under leaves. When the **tadpoles** hatch, they stick themselves to the **back** of a parent. The parent carries them to a small pool of water, for example in a plant where rainwater has collected. There the tadpoles keep growing until they become small frogs.

gewusst: Some poison dart frogs carry their tadpoles right up into the treetops, where rainwater collects in plants.
Researchers study the frogs’ poison because new medicines might perhaps be made from it.

teile.einleitung: Photovoltaics means turning sunlight directly into electric current. This happens in solar cells, which are usually made of silicon. In Switzerland many new systems are built every year on roofs, façades and even dam walls.
wichtigste: A photovoltaic system turns sunlight directly into electricity.
Solar cells are usually made of silicon.
Many solar cells together make up a solar module.
An inverter turns the direct current into alternating current for the socket.
Photovoltaics produces no exhaust gases while operating.
In Switzerland many new systems are added every year.

abschnitte.text: The word **photovoltaics** is made up of the Greek word for light and the name of the unit **volt**. When light falls on a **solar cell**, tiny particles inside it, the electrons, are set in motion. This produces electric current. The cell needs no moving parts for this, and it works quietly and without exhaust gases.

Most solar cells are made of **silicon**. This is a material obtained from quartz sand. Many cells are put together to make a **solar module**, the familiar dark panels. Several modules form a **photovoltaic system**. The cells deliver **direct current**. A device called an **inverter** turns it into alternating current, as it comes out of the socket.

In Switzerland many new systems are built every year, mainly on **house roofs**, barns and factory halls. The electricity can be used by the owners or fed into the grid. Photovoltaics is an important part of the Confederation’s **Energy Strategy 2050**. With it, Switzerland wants to get more of its electricity from renewable sources. Systems are also being built in the mountains, for example on the dam wall of the **Muttsee** in the canton of Glarus.

Sunlight is free and never runs out. A system produces no CO2 while operating. However, it only delivers electricity when it is light: not at all at night, and less in winter. That is why **storage**, for example batteries, and other power stations are also needed. In the mountains the sun often shines above the fog in winter, and snow reflects extra light back.

gewusst: The French physicist Alexandre Edmond Becquerel discovered as early as 1839 that light can produce an electric voltage in certain materials.
Space probes and satellites in space also often get their electricity from solar cells.

teile.einleitung: Peak oil is the point at which oil production reaches its maximum and then begins to fall. The idea comes from the geologist M. King Hubbert. People still debate whether supplies will run short first or whether demand will fall before that happens.
wichtigste: Peak oil is the maximum of oil production, after which output declines.
In 1956 M. King Hubbert predicted that US production would peak around 1970.
The Hubbert curve is bell-shaped.
Reserves are deposits that can be extracted profitably with today’s technology.
Britain reached its production peak in the North Sea in 1999.
Thanks to fracking, US production passed its 1970 record in 2018.
With “peak demand”, demand falls before oil becomes scarce.

abschnitte.text: The geologist **Marion King Hubbert** worked for the oil company Shell. In 1956 he presented a model: production from an oil field first rises, reaches a **maximum** and then falls again at a similar speed. This produces a **bell-shaped curve**. Hubbert predicted that the USA would reach its production peak around 1970. Conventional US production did in fact peak in 1970.

Experts distinguish between two terms. **Reserves** are proven deposits that can be extracted profitably at today’s prices and with today’s technology. **Resources** also include amounts that are only suspected or that are not currently economic. The **static range** is reserves divided by annual production. For example: 1,750 billion barrels divided by 35 billion barrels a year gives 50 years. New discoveries and changes in consumption are not taken into account.

British oil production in the **North Sea** reached its maximum in **1999** and has fallen sharply since then. Norway followed in 2001. If the output of an oil field falls by 5 per cent every year, after two years it is not 90 but 0.95 × 0.95 = **90.25 per cent** of the original. Percentage declines are multiplied, not added. In the USA things turned out differently from what was expected: **fracking** made it possible to extract oil from shale rock, and in 2018 production passed the 1970 record for the first time.

Extracting oil takes energy in itself. The figure **EROI** (Energy Return on Investment) compares the energy gained with the energy used. The harder the oil is to reach, for example from **oil sands** or the deep sea, the smaller this ratio becomes. As early as 1972, the report **“The Limits to Growth”** by the Club of Rome made the finite nature of raw materials a worldwide topic. It used computer models to study population, production and the use of raw materials.

With **peak oil**, geology limits production. With **peak demand**, on the other hand, need falls first, even though there would still be enough oil. Reasons can be **electric cars**, more economical appliances and climate policy. Experts do not agree on when, or which, of the two peaks will arrive worldwide. Switzerland also wants to reduce its use of fossil energy, for example with heat pumps instead of oil heating.

gewusst: A barrel holds about 159 litres.
Switzerland produces no crude oil of its own and has to import all of it.
